beliefs.practice: Use a single, process‑wide MongoClient (singleton) that is reused for all requests instead of opening a new connection per operation; configure maxPoolSize (e.g., 50) and minPoolSize (e.g., 0) rather than creating/destroying clients repeatedly.

Require TLS/SSL for all connections (include tls=true or tlsCertificateFile as needed) and never disable certificate validation in production; enforce tls/ssl in the connection string and in driver options.

Keep the cluster connection string/credentials out of source code and version control: store the DOCUMENTDB_URI and any DB credentials in Azure Key Vault or a secrets manager and only expose short‑lived secrets to the runtime environment.

Use least‑privilege database accounts: create an application user with only the necessary roles (read/write to the app database and specific collections) rather than using the account with the cluster admin/primary key.

Configure sensible driver timeouts and retry settings: set serverSelectionTimeoutMS (e.g., 30s), connectTimeoutMS (e.g., 10s), socketTimeoutMS, and enable retryWrites where supported; implement exponential backoff for higher‑level retry logic.

Handle rate limits and throttling (HTTP 429): detect 429 responses or explicit throttling errors, respect Retry‑After when provided, and perform exponential backoff with jitter rather than immediate retry loops.
Make seed and migration scripts idempotent (use upsert or check-and-insert) so repeated runs against the same database do not create duplicates or corrupt sample data.

Design collections and document schemas around query patterns: keep frequently queried keys at the top level (e.g., claimId, transactionId, status, createdAt) to avoid expensive subdocument scans and to enable simple indexes.

Create explicit indexes for filter and sort patterns used by the app — e.g., an index on { claimId: 1 }, a compound index on { transactionId: 1, timestamp: -1 }, and an index on decision status + updatedAt — and verify with explain() that queries use those indexes.
Use TTL indexes for ephemeral records (logs, temporary evidence caches, or retries) so old debugging/evidence documents are expired automatically rather than accumulating indefinitely.

Store vector embeddings in a dedicated field (e.g., embedding: [Float32,...]) and create the cluster’s vector index on that field with the algorithm and parameters (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN) tuned for expected vector dimensionality and query latency/recall.

When using vector similarity with cosine distance, normalize embeddings before storage (or use the index’s appropriate distance metric) and choose index parameters (efConstruction/efSearch, M, quantization) appropriate to recall vs latency tradeoffs.

Keep individual documents well under the BSON document size limit (16 MB); if evidence has large attachments (documents, PDFs), store them external to DocumentDB (blob storage) and store references/metadata in the database.

Use collection-level validation rules (JSON Schema validator) to enforce required fields and types for critical collections (claims, transactions, decisions) so malformed documents are rejected at write time.

Avoid multi-document transactions unless necessary; if you need atomicity across collections use transactions with explicit startTransaction/commit and set writeConcern appropriately, but be aware of performance and support limits on the provider.

Set an appropriate write concern (acknowledged or majority depending on durability needs) and use readPreference primary for fresh reads after writes (or primaryPreferred when allowing read replicas for lower latency), to avoid eventual-consistency surprises in a multi-agent orchestration.

Log and redact PII and secrets: when persisting debug information or decision traces, remove or hash personally identifiable information (account numbers, card numbers) and never log the raw DOCUMENTDB_URI or DB credentials.

Run explain() on representative queries and monitor index usage and slow query logs; iterate indexes based on real query plans rather than adding every possible index upfront to avoid write amplification.

For CI/unit tests, mock the MongoDB client calls and rely on a small set of integration/e2e tests that run explicitly against the live cluster (guarded by env var) so automated tests do not require cloud credentials by default.
Avoid unbounded result sets: always page queries (limit + sort + range filter or use cursor.batchSize) and prevent server-side scans that return million-row results into the app memory.

Protect against injection and malformed queries by validating and whitelisting queryable fields (do not accept raw query JSON from untrusted inputs), and use parameterized queries / typed filters instead of building query strings.

When writing decision outcomes (accept/reject), write idempotently (upsert with a unique business key like claimId) and include metadata (decisionBy, decisionAt, reason, evidenceIds) to support auditing and future re-evaluation.

Monitor cluster resource metrics (CPU, disk, memory, index usage, IOPS/throughput, vector index build progress) and set alerts for high RU/s or throttling; scale compute/indexing tiers before hitting capacity for production workloads.

For vectors and semantic search, validate embeddings at ingest (correct dimensionality, no NaN/Inf) and store metadata such as model name and dimensionality alongside each vector so future re-indexing/search is consistent.

Use explainable, auditable decision records: keep the policyAgent's reasoning snippet (or a hash of it) plus the deterministic fallback path when OpenAI is not available, and do not depend solely on ephemeral LLM responses to justify recorded decisions.
